Summary:
This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features. The authors argue that although recent CBMs can match feature-based classifiers on source-domain accuracy, they can degrade substantially under distribution shift. They identify three failure modes—non-robust concept bottlenecks under low-level shift, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers under concept-level shift, and incomplete concept sets—and propose CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data. CONDA consists of concept-score alignment (CSA), linear probing adaptation (LPA), and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB). Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, sometimes approaching non-interpretable baselines.

Overall assessment:
The paper addresses an interesting and timely problem at the intersection of interpretability, foundation models, and test-time adaptation. The high-level motivation is strong: if CBMs are to be useful in deployment, they should remain both accurate and interpretable under shift. The proposed decomposition of adaptation into concept-bank adaptation, classifier adaptation, and residual concept expansion is intuitive and reasonably well aligned with the identified failure modes. Empirically, the method appears effective in several settings, especially on concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.

That said, I have several concerns about the technical framing, evaluation methodology, and some claims around interpretability and robustness. The paper is promising, but I do not think the current version fully substantiates all of its claims.

Strengths:

1. Important problem setting.
The paper tackles a meaningful gap: CBMs under distribution shift, especially in a source-free test-time adaptation regime. This is a natural and practically relevant setting.

2. Clear modular method.
The three-part structure of CONDA is easy to understand and maps well onto the proposed failure modes. This modularity is also useful for ablations.

3. Broad empirical coverage.
The experiments span multiple datasets, shift types, backbones, and CBM construction methods. This breadth is a strong point.

4. Good empirical gains in several cases.
The improvements on Waterbirds and Metashift are substantial, and the component analysis suggests that different modules matter under different shifts.

5. Interesting interpretability angle.
The residual concept branch is a nice idea for handling incomplete concept sets, and the qualitative claim that new bird-related concepts emerge on Waterbirds is compelling.

Weaknesses and concerns:

1. The formalization of shift types is not fully convincing.
The paper defines low-level shift as one that leaves the concept-score distribution unchanged, and concept-level shift as one that changes concept scores but not prediction distributions. These definitions are neat mathematically, but they are not really operational in practice. In fact, much of the paper’s motivation is that under “low-level shifts” the concept-score distribution often does change because the concept extractor is not robust. So the formal definitions and the empirical usage are somewhat mismatched. The taxonomy is useful as intuition, but it is not a rigorous characterization of the actual benchmark shifts used.

2. Heavy reliance on pseudo-labels from non-interpretable models.
A central practical issue is that adaptation depends on pseudo-labels from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors on the FM features. This raises two concerns:
- First, much of the adaptation signal comes from non-interpretable predictors rather than from the CBM itself.
- Second, if those predictors are already strong under shift, then CONDA may be inheriting their robustness rather than demonstrating intrinsic robustness of concept-based adaptation.
This does not invalidate the method, but it weakens the claim that the CBM itself is being adapted in a principled way. The paper should more clearly position CONDA as a pseudo-label distillation/adaptation method from FM-based predictors into a CBM.

3. Source-free assumption is somewhat softened by retained source statistics.
CSA assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source concept scores, i.e., means and covariances for every class. While this is lighter than retaining source data, it is still nontrivial source information. In some settings, storing per-class covariance matrices may be impractical or privacy-sensitive. The paper should discuss this more explicitly and compare against variants using weaker source summaries.

4. Interpretability claims are only partially supported.
The paper claims that CONDA yields “concept-based interpretations better aligned with the test data,” but the evidence presented in the main text is mostly qualitative. There is no strong quantitative evaluation of interpretability quality, concept faithfulness, concept stability, or human alignment. Also, the residual concepts are initialized randomly and optimized for predictive performance with regularizers; whether they correspond to semantically meaningful concepts consistently is unclear. The automated annotation procedure is mentioned only in the appendix. This is not enough to support broad interpretability claims.

5. Some results suggest instability or degradation.
The method does not uniformly help. For example, on CIFAR100 with Yeh et al. concepts, CONDA slightly hurts AVG and WG. On Camelyon17 with Yeh et al., adaptation also degrades performance. On Waterbirds, CONDA does not match the LP baseline and even underperforms zero-shot AVG. These are important caveats because the abstract and introduction emphasize alignment with non-interpretable classification. That statement seems too strong as a general conclusion.

6. Fairness of comparisons is not entirely clear.
The paper compares adapted CBMs against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines, but it does not compare against generic TTA methods applied directly to the CBM or to the FM+linear head pipeline in a matched setting. Since the paper claims to be the first TTA method for CBMs, a stronger baseline suite is needed:
- Tent/MEMO/CoTTA-style adaptation on the CBM classifier
- adaptation of the FM+linear probe baseline under the same pseudo-labeling regime
- perhaps adaptation of post-hoc CBM weights only, without concept adaptation
Without these, it is hard to isolate how much of the gain comes from the specific CBM-aware design versus standard adaptation machinery.

7. The residual branch may dilute the bottleneck interpretation.
Equation (5) shows that the final predictor is effectively a larger linear model over original plus residual concepts. If the residual concepts are numerous or weakly interpretable, the model may become less interpretable than the original CBM. The paper argues the opposite, but this tradeoff is not quantified. How sparse are the residual weights? How often do residual concepts dominate predictions? How semantically coherent are they across runs?

8. Methodological details are missing from the main paper.
Several important details appear deferred to appendices: hyperparameter selection, number of residual concepts, batch sizes, number of gradient steps, computational overhead, and concept annotation. Since TTA methods can be sensitive to these choices, the main paper should include at least a concise summary. It is especially important to know whether hyperparameters were tuned on target-domain labels, shift-specific validation sets, or source-only heuristics.

9. Statistical reporting could be stronger.
The table reports means and standard deviations, but significance is not discussed. Some gains are small, and some degradations are non-negligible. It would help to report the number of runs consistently and perhaps confidence intervals or paired significance tests.

10. Novelty is moderate rather than high.
The overall recipe combines known ingredients: pseudo-labeling, class-aware alignment via Mahalanobis distances, linear-head adaptation, and residual concept expansion. The novelty lies mainly in tailoring these to CBMs and organizing them around failure modes. That is still valuable, but the paper should avoid overstating conceptual novelty.

Questions for the authors:

1. How are hyperparameters selected in the source-free setting? Are any target labels or validation splits used?
2. How sensitive is CONDA to pseudo-label quality? What happens if only zero-shot or only LP pseudo-labels are used?
3. How much source information is required in practice for CSA? Could diagonal covariances or class prototypes suffice?
4. How many residual concepts are added, and how sensitive are results to r?
5. Do residual concepts remain semantically stable across random seeds?
6. Can standard TTA baselines applied to the CBM or FM+LP pipeline recover similar gains?
7. What fraction of final prediction mass comes from the residual branch versus the original concept bank?

Suggestions for improvement:

1. Strengthen baselines.
Include standard TTA methods adapted to:
- the FM+LP baseline,
- the CBM classifier only,
- the CBM concept bank only,
under the same unlabeled target setting.

2. Clarify the role of pseudo-labels.
Add ablations comparing:
- self-labeling from the CBM,
- zero-shot only,
- LP only,
- ensemble pseudo-labeling.
This would clarify where the gains come from.

3. Better support interpretability claims.
Provide quantitative analyses such as:
- concept sparsity before/after adaptation,
- concept coherence scores,
- overlap with human-annotated concepts,
- stability of top concepts across runs,
- fraction of predictions relying on residual concepts.

4. Discuss source-statistics assumptions more carefully.
Ablate full covariance vs diagonal covariance vs class means only, and discuss storage/privacy implications.

5. Tighten claims in abstract and conclusion.
The current wording suggests broad alignment with non-interpretable classifiers, but the results are mixed. The claims should be made more precise.

6. Improve theoretical framing.
Either soften the formal definitions as motivating abstractions or connect them more directly to measurable properties in the experiments.

Minor comments:

1. There are a few notation/presentation issues. For example, Eq. (5) is later referred to as Eq. (3) in Section 3.2/Algorithm references, which is confusing.
2. The Mahalanobis distance expression appears to have a parenthesis typo in Section 3.1.
3. The paper sometimes uses “concept-level shift” in a benchmark-specific sense and sometimes in a formal distributional sense; this should be harmonized.
4. AVG and WG are described as per-class metrics, but for Waterbirds and related datasets group structure is often more nuanced than class alone; please clarify exactly how groups are defined.
5. The claim “first approach” should be softened unless the literature search is exhaustive.

Recommendation:
Weak Accept / Borderline

Rationale:
I like the problem, the modular method is sensible, and the empirical results are often strong. I also think the paper could stimulate useful follow-up work on robust interpretable adaptation. However, the current version overclaims in a few places, relies heavily on pseudo-labels from non-interpretable predictors, and does not yet provide enough evidence for its interpretability claims or enough baseline comparisons to fully validate the CBM-specific contribution. If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the framing and strengthen the empirical analysis accordingly.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. The authors argue that although FM-based CBMs can be interpretable and competitive in-source, they often degrade substantially under deployment shifts. They categorize failure modes into non-robust concept mappings under low-level shifts, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers under concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets. To address these, they propose CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: concept-score alignment (CSA) to adapt concept vectors via class-conditional Gaussian statistics and Mahalanobis losses, linear probing adaptation (LPA) to adapt the concept-to-label layer using pseudo-labels, and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) to add new concepts for missing target-domain semantics. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs in many settings, especially under concept-level shifts, and qualitative evidence suggests adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: making FM-based concept bottleneck models adaptive under test-time distribution shift while preserving interpretability.
Clear decomposition of failure modes into concept misalignment, classifier mismatch, and concept incompleteness, which motivates the three-part method design.
Method is modular and practically appealing: adapts only the CBM components while keeping the foundation model frozen and requiring no source data during adaptation.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, shift types, FM backbones, and CBM construction methods, which strengthens the claim of broad applicability.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs in several challenging settings, especially Waterbirds and Metashift, where gains are substantial.
Component-wise analysis is useful and supports the intuition that different adaptation stages matter for different shift types.
The residual concept branch is an interesting idea for handling incomplete concept sets and potentially improving both robustness and interpretability.
Paper is generally well written, with intuitive figures and a coherent narrative connecting theory, method, and experiments.
weaknesses: The theoretical formalization of shift types is somewhat idealized and not tightly connected to the actual optimization objectives or guarantees of the method.

The approach relies heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictions; if these are poor under shift, adaptation may reinforce errors, and this dependency is not deeply analyzed in the main paper.
CSA assumes class-conditional Gaussian concept-score distributions and access to source-domain class statistics; the realism and sensitivity of this assumption are not fully justified.

Comparisons are mostly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines, but there is limited direct comparison to stronger generic test-time adaptation baselines applied to the same CBM pipeline.

Some reported results show adaptation hurting performance relative to the unadapted CBM (e.g., certain CIFAR100 and Camelyon/Yeh cases), suggesting instability or mismatch that deserves more discussion.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative; there is no rigorous quantitative evaluation of whether adapted or residual concepts are truly more human-aligned or faithful.
The online adaptation protocol may be sensitive to batch order and batch composition, but robustness to these factors is not clearly established in the main text.
The method introduces several stages and hyperparameters, increasing complexity and making it harder to isolate which parts are essential in practice.
soundness_issues: The definition of low-level shift assumes invariant concept-score distributions, but in practice low-level perturbations often alter FM features and concept projections; thus the formal categorization is more descriptive than a sound modeling assumption.

CSA minimizes a log ratio of intra/inter-class Mahalanobis distances using pseudo-labels, but there is no argument that this objective consistently estimates alignment to the source conditional distributions, especially under pseudo-label noise.

The source-free setting still assumes availability of source-domain class-conditional means and covariances of concept scores; this is reasonable but should be treated as an additional retained artifact from training, not pure source-free adaptation.
The Gaussian modeling of concept scores may be poor for sparse or highly non-linear concept spaces, and covariance estimation can be unstable, especially for many classes or limited source samples.

RCB is motivated as adding missing concepts, but the learned residual vectors are optimized primarily for predictive performance with weak regularization; there is limited evidence they correspond to semantically coherent concepts beyond selected examples.

Because adaptation is online and uses pseudo-labels from FM predictors, improvements may partly reflect distillation from stronger non-interpretable predictors rather than intrinsic CBM adaptation; this confound is not fully disentangled.
